stem: Three independent events A, B, and C have probabilities P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 1/3, and P(C) = 1/4. What is the probability that exactly one of the three events occurs?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Computing P(at least one) = 1 - P(none) = 1 - (1/2)(2/3)(3/4) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4, solving for at-least-one instead of exactly-one.
Computing P(all three occur) = P(A)*P(B)*P(C) = (1/2)(1/3)(1/4) = 1/24, solving for all-three instead of exactly-one.
Computing only the P(only A) = (1/2)(2/3)(3/4) = 1/4 term without adding the other two exactly-one terms.

explanation: P(exactly one) requires summing three mutually exclusive terms: A occurs while B and C do not, plus B occurs while A and C do not, plus C occurs while A and B do not. Each term multiplies the relevant probabilities using independence. Sum = 6/24 + 3/24 + 2/24 = 11/24.

explanation_sections.punchline: Exactly-one means one event fires and the other two do not, requiring three separate product terms.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the model: exactly-one for independent events = sum of three disjoint scenarios. P(A only) = (1/2)(2/3)(3/4) = 1/4; P(B only) = (1/2)(1/3)(3/4) = 1/8; P(C only) = (1/2)(2/3)(1/4) = 1/12. Common denominator 24: 6+3+2 = 11/24.
explanation_sections.lesson: Exactly-one is not the same as at-least-one: you must multiply in the complement of each non-occurring event.
explanation_sections.timing: 100 seconds. Work through all three cases systematically. The trap is stopping after one term (1/4) or computing at-least-one instead (3/4).
